title: Chinese research ships lingered over undersea cables near Taiwan, analysts say
dek: A geospatial firm says four Chinese survey ships slowed and stopped along cable routes since May, as Manila and Tokyo raise similar alarms. India, whose data runs through a few landing points, has watched such ships in its own waters.
author: Declaration Desk
body:
Four Chinese scientific research ships have moved in unusual patterns over the routes of undersea internet cables around Taiwan since May, slowing sharply, stopping for long periods and turning irregularly, according to an analysis by the geospatial intelligence firm ingeniSPACE reported in a Japanese newspaper this week. The firm said China appeared to be gathering information on undersea infrastructure along the "first island chain" that could be used in grey-zone operations or a sudden crisis.

The findings come days after the Philippine Coast Guard said Chinese research vessels had been surveying cable routes near the Philippines, Taiwan and Japan without permission from those governments. Undersea cables carry the great majority of international internet and phone traffic, and the reports add to concern across Asia, India included, about how exposed that infrastructure is.

## What the analysis found

ingeniSPACE compared the ships' Automatic Identification System (AIS) tracking data with known cable routes, according to the newspaper's report as republished elsewhere. It named the ships as the Xiangyanghong 22, Jia Geng, Mushanzi and Tongji. The places where all four stopped or slowed coincided with cables linking Taiwan to Japan, the US, Singapore and the Philippines, in waters north and east of Taiwan and in the Bashi Channel to the south. About 24 cables run near Taiwan, 14 of them international links.

The firm reported similar behaviour off Japan: since 2024, research vessels affiliated with a Chinese university have repeatedly slowed, stopped and turned sharply in international waters east of Hokkaido and inside Japan's exclusive economic zone off Nagoya, where their movements overlapped with identified cables, the newspaper reported.

A Taiwanese government official told the newspaper that the analysis broadly matched what Taiwan's authorities had found. Chisako Masuo, a professor at Kyushu University, said the ships might be preparing for a possible conflict over Taiwan or a US-China confrontation.

## Manila and Tokyo

The Philippine Coast Guard said a Chinese research vessel, the Jia Hai Ke 7, spent several days from late September surveying inside the Philippine exclusive economic zone around the Batanes Islands without Manila's permission. When Philippine patrol craft approached, two China Coast Guard ships moved in to escort it. The coast guard said the vessel was reportedly owned by a private Chinese company; its spokesman, Jay Tarriela, said in October that ships loitering at fixed points could pose a risk to cables and that the data they collect could be used for military purposes.

Japan's Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi told the upper house on 9 October that undersea cables were critical infrastructure and that "a certain risk of damage exists". Her government is moving to put their protection under state-led management.

## Beijing's position

The Declaration found no response from China's foreign ministry to the latest analysis. Beijing has consistently rejected accusations that Chinese ships have deliberately damaged undersea cables, and it has described the vessels involved as privately owned civilian ships. After Manila and Taipei coordinated on cable security last month, Beijing warned the Philippines to "strictly adhere to the One-China Principle". Hu Xijin, a former editor of a state-run Chinese newspaper, wrote on Weibo that the data the ships gather could also serve defensive purposes.

## Why it matters for India

India depends on undersea cables for almost all of its international data, and its links are concentrated at a few landing points, chiefly Mumbai and Chennai. Analysts have long urged New Delhi to spread its cable routes and treat landing stations as critical infrastructure.

Chinese survey and research ships have been a recurring concern in the Indian Ocean as well. India objected in 2022 when the Chinese tracking ship Yuan Wang 5 docked at Sri Lanka's Hambantota port, and Sri Lanka imposed a year-long moratorium on foreign research ships in January 2024. New Delhi has worried that seabed data gathered by such vessels could help submarine operations, one report has said; China's foreign ministry has said their research is peaceful and scientific.

## What happens next

Taiwan's Mainland Affairs Council has said it expects China to use more non-military vessels to press maritime claims against Taiwan, Japan and the Philippines. Japan's budget request for 2027 includes money for cable-laying ships and for surveillance and cybersecurity at cable landing stations.
